idiom_name: request.user / request.auser() with AnonymousUser for unauthenticated requests
implementation_notes: The descriptor is the framework's user object on the request: AuthenticationMiddleware sets request.user to the configured AUTH_USER_MODEL instance (AnonymousUser when nobody is logged in) and request.auser() is the async-friendly accessor; consumers ask is_authenticated and then read id, roles, tenant or permissions from that object. Middleware plus a user model replaces the classic authenticator/descriptor/factory trio, and the object is reloaded from the session per request, so revocation takes effect on the next request. Hand-roll a dataclass descriptor only when the service has no framework user model, and keep it a thin adapter over the model rather than a second identity.
pitfalls: request.user is lazy and needs SessionMiddleware plus AuthenticationMiddleware; reading it in a non-request context raises ImproperlyConfigured, and async views must await request.auser().
AnonymousUser is a real object with is_authenticated == False, not None: treating missing authentication as None leads to AttributeError inside guards.
Django caches request.user per request, so a role change or sign-out during the request is not visible - do not keep the user object beyond the request.

variants.name: Flask-Login current_user proxy
variants.implementation_notes: Flask-Login supplies the descriptor as a context-local proxy: current_user resolves to whatever the registered user_loader returns for the id stored in the session, or AnonymousUserMixin when nobody is logged in; login_user()/logout_user() manage the session and @login_required / fresh_login_required guard routes. The proxy plus a loader callback replaces the classic descriptor object, and the user is loaded from your store per request, so the session carries only an identifier. Prefer this variant in Flask apps; pass the user explicitly where no request context exists, such as background jobs or Celery tasks.
pitfalls: current_user is a LocalProxy: outside a request or app context (background thread, Celery worker, popped teardown) accessing it raises RuntimeError - pass the user object explicitly there.
The loader must return None for unknown ids instead of raising: Flask-Login then treats the session as anonymous, whereas an exception turns every request into a 500.
Mutating current_user's attributes does not persist beyond the request, and with an ORM entity it may even be flushed accidentally.
